q: We fought constantly over the rules. "You're picking him up too much." "Don't let him sleep next to you, you'll ruin the progress." Every time things slipped for a day or two, which, again, is totally normal for a 4 to 5 month old, we'd turn on each other. "It's because YOU broke the routine."
cx: Father's long story of a 17-month-old; ends by linking a tracking app (possible promotion).

q: a bad night or two doesn't undo anything. It's a baby, not a spreadsheet. Consistency over weeks is what matters.
cx: Same father on what he would tell them both in hindsight.

q: Half my stress wasn't the lack of sleep, it was not knowing whether something was actually WRONG. Having real numbers to compare against killed that anxiety.
cx: Same father crediting a predictive tracking app, later named as hushly.app.

q: I just want to express my gratitude to the person who suggested I work on the baby’s schedule two months ago before attempting sleep training.

q: I used to go to bed at 7:30 p.m. with her because she couldn’t sleep alone.  Now, I feel more present, and she’s resting better.

q: a combination of parental illness, baby illness, ill-planned travel, and a night-pooping phase all contributed to a sleep training journey lasting over a month instead of the oft-promised 3-5 days.

q: it can become a bit of a circular spiral where because it's taking longer, you as parents get more tired and burnt out and so have less willpower at night

q: Nursing was the only form of comfort she’d accept - everything else made her scream bloody murder. It got worse when she was teething, sometimes I was up 7-8 times a night. I tried SO many things.

q: This is my second baby and my first was an angel sleeper, so I was humbled big time!

q: every time he was teething or when he got sick, we had to resleep train him afterward. I felt like I was just torturing the little guy and he grew to hate bedtime (and so did I).

q: I finally leaned into my maternal instincts and allowed him to nurse to sleep one night. He only woke up once and he didn’t cry at all.

q: I just wanted to post this in case there were any moms who were pushed by their pediatrician or friends to sleep train. I fell into the idea that if you don’t sleep train, you’re a bad mom setting your kid up for failure.

q: We attempted the Ferber Method but when my husband did a check in at 10 minutes the crying got significantly worse so we switched to CIO. He fell asleep after 53 minutes of crying.

q: the advice i got, overwhelmingly, was to keep him awake longer, to push his wake windows further, to ignore his sleepy cues and aim for a later bedtime. some of this worked. some of it really did not.
